Index of coincidence: a reproducible rune baseline

Matching-pair counts for every archived page, exact inputs, scaling, invariants and interpretation limits.

The index of coincidence (IoC) measures how often two different positions in a text contain the same symbol. It summarizes the symbol distribution; it does not read the text or identify a cipher by itself. This guide provides a reproducible whole-page baseline for the archived Liber Primus runes.

Count matching pairs

Before using this number to compare candidate decodings, read what cipher operations preserve. A rearrangement or fixed reversible alphabet substitution cannot change whole-stream IoC.

Let N be the number of runes and nᵢ the count of rune i. The unscaled convention used here is:

IoC = sum(nᵢ × (nᵢ − 1)) / (N × (N − 1))

There are N × (N − 1) ordered choices of two distinct positions. A rune occurring nᵢ times contributes nᵢ × (nᵢ − 1) matching choices. Dividing gives the probability of a match when sampling positions without replacement. Counting unordered pairs instead divides both quantities by two and produces the same result.

For the three-symbol sequence F F U, only the two F positions match. The numerator is 2 and the denominator is 6, so IoC is 1/3. For F U it is 0; for F F it is 1. With zero or one symbol there is no pair to draw, so IoC is undefined. The JSON uses null in that case.

Exactly what this baseline counts

Each page is measured separately using its archived text/lp…txt file.
Only the 29 symbols in the published rune alphabet count. A rune with a multi-letter Latin label is still one symbol.
All archived runes count, including rune headings. Punctuation, whitespace, line-wrap markers, Latin text and printed decimal numbers do not.
No transcription corrections, decryption, heading removal or page concatenation are applied. This is an archived-stream baseline, not a plaintext baseline.
A page with no archived rune transcription and a recorded count of zero has an undefined IoC. This does not imply that its image or embedded payload has no information.

Every record contains the input path and SHA-256, the rune count, a 29-entry frequency array, the numerator, denominator and IoC. The array follows the alphabet order stored in the same report. Its alphabet hash covers the UTF-8 concatenation of those 29 runes without separators. Unknown symbols in the Unicode Runic block cause an error rather than being silently discarded.

Reproduce the results

python scripts/rune_ioc.py lp2-31
python scripts/rune_ioc.py --check
python scripts/rune_ioc.py --output my-rune-ioc.json
python scripts/test_rune_ioc.py

Run from the repository or the extracted reference-data ZIP with Python 3; no extra packages, network access or AI are required. See script setup. The first command prints a single-page report. The second recomputes all 75 records and compares them with the published baseline. The third writes a complete report and refuses to overwrite an existing file. The fourth checks short controls, invariants and an independent enumeration of matching pairs.

Download the calculation script · Download all page results and input hashes. The reference-data ZIP includes the script and its inputs; downloading the script alone does not include the manuscript transcriptions.

Examples from the archived streams

	Page	Runes	Unscaled IoC

	LP1-00	0	Undefined

	LP1-01	184	0.06402946

	LP2-31	269	0.03295789

	LP2-57	95	0.06270997


These are rounded display values. Use the integer numerator and denominator in the report for exact comparisons. The examples illustrate different input lengths and values; they are not a selection of statistically significant pages.

See the distributions behind the numbers
Archived-stream frequencies for LP2-31 and LP2-57. Bars show the proportion of each rune, not raw counts. Open or save the full-size SVG; use the alphabet reference to look up an index.

LP2-31’s counts range from 5 to 13 per rune. LP2-57 has seven runes with no occurrences and one rune, index 18, with 15 occurrences. Concentration matters because a count contributes nᵢ(nᵢ − 1) matching pairs: a count of 15 supplies 210, while a count of 5 supplies only 20. Large counts therefore contribute disproportionately to IoC.

The dashed line is the equal-probability reference, 1/29 per rune. It is not a confidence bound or a minimum. A bar above it simply means that this rune occurs more often than the uniform proportion in this sample. The two pages have different lengths, and the chart does not estimate how surprising either distribution is.

To redraw the figure, extract the reference-data ZIP, install Matplotlib with python -m pip install matplotlib, then run:

python scripts/rune_ioc.py --check
python scripts/plot_rune_frequencies.py --output my-rune-frequencies.svg

The first command checks the saved counts against the archived inputs. The second reads those saved counts and renders the chart, refusing to overwrite an existing output. Matplotlib is needed only to redraw the figure; the numerical IoC checks use Python’s standard library. The plotting script fixes the axes and page selection so the two panels remain comparable.

What is the reference level?

For independent, uniformly distributed symbols from a 29-symbol alphabet, the expected match probability is 1/29 ≈ 0.03448276. This follows by adding the 29 possible matching outcomes, each with probability (1/29)². A finite sample need not equal this expectation. An observed value below it is possible; LP2-31 is one example.

The report also supplies scaled_ioc_29 = 29 × IoC, whose uniform independent expectation is 1. Always state whether a number is scaled. Do not compare this rune statistic directly with an English A–Z benchmark: the alphabet, multi-letter symbols, encoding and inclusion rules differ.

What it can and cannot distinguish

Reordering a fixed set of symbols leaves its frequency counts unchanged. A transposition therefore preserves whole-stream IoC. A one-to-one substitution renames symbols but preserves their multiplicities, so it also preserves IoC. This includes Atbash and a constant modular shift. Equality of IoC does not establish which of these transformations, if any, was used.

A changing substitution, such as a repeating-key Vigenère operation, can change the distribution. A value near the uniform reference is nevertheless not proof of Vigenère, randomness or strong encryption. A higher value does not prove plaintext or a monoalphabetic cipher. Different processes can produce similar frequency distributions.

Whole-page measurements can mix regions with different rules. A heading may be unencrypted while the body is encrypted. Joining pages introduces cross-page pairs, so the combined IoC is not generally the simple average of page values. A corrected glyph can change counts. Record these choices before comparing results.

Turning a baseline into an experiment

A periodic analysis would divide positions into columns under a stated period and starting offset, then compare column distributions. That is a separate procedure from the whole-page calculation here. It requires explicit punctuation handling, page boundaries, column lengths and an aggregation rule. Testing many periods and reporting only the largest value creates a selection effect.

Before making a significance claim, specify a null model that matches the actual question. Shuffling the same rune stream cannot test whether its global IoC is unusual, because every shuffle has exactly the same counts. It can be useful for an order-sensitive statistic, such as a specified column analysis, but that experiment needs its own recorded method and results.

This baseline reports descriptive measurements only. It supplies no p-values, cipher classification, key-length estimate or new solution. A technique search belongs in Have we tried it? only when its scope and results are documented through the experiment process.

A worked example: splitting a trial period into columns

In a simple repeating-key cipher, positions separated by one key period use the same key symbol. Testing a period of two therefore groups positions 0, 2, 4, … into one column and positions 1, 3, 5, … into another. If the proposed period and key-advance rule are right, each column receives a constant shift, which preserves its IoC. This explains why column measurements can be useful; it does not make the highest-scoring trial period the correct one.

Use the invented sequence F U F U F F U. These are seven single-symbol labels for a teaching example, not text from a Liber Primus page. Indexing starts at zero:

	Column	Positions	Symbols	Matching ordered pairs	All ordered pairs	IoC

	0	0, 2, 4, 6	F F F U	6	12	1/2

	1	1, 3, 5	U U F	2	6	1/3


There are two different ways to combine these values. The ordinary mean gives each column equal weight: (1/2 + 1/3) / 2 = 5/12 ≈ 0.4167. A pooled pair rate gives each eligible within-column pair equal weight: (6 + 2) / (12 + 6) = 4/9 ≈ 0.4444. The larger column has twice as many ordered pairs, so it contributes twice the weight to the pooled rate.

Pooled column IoC =
    sum(column matching-pair counts)
    / sum(column ordered-pair counts)

Neither number is the whole-sequence IoC. Across all seven positions there are four F symbols and three U symbols, giving (4 × 3 + 3 × 2) / (7 × 6) = 3/7. The whole-sequence denominator includes pairs whose positions belong to different columns. The pooled column denominator excludes them.

Why shuffling matters for columns but not the total

Rearrange the same seven symbols as F F U U F F U. The whole-sequence counts stay four F and three U, so whole-sequence IoC remains 3/7. But the two columns become F U F U and F U F; both have IoC 1/3, and their pooled rate is also 1/3.

This is the distinction a shuffle experiment uses. It preserves the global symbol distribution while changing where symbols fall. A randomization test of column structure can compare an observed column statistic with shuffled versions. It cannot test whether the global IoC itself is unusual under that same shuffle, because that statistic never changes.

For unequal column sizes, specify whether you use the ordinary mean or the pooled rate. A column with fewer than two symbols has no pair and contributes zero to both pooled counts; if every column is that short, the pooled rate is undefined. Very short columns also give unstable estimates, so adding more trial periods is not automatically adding more information.

Reproduce the small example

Save this self-contained Python example as ioc-columns-example.py and run python ioc-columns-example.py. It uses exact fractions and no manuscript inputs or external packages.

from collections import Counter
from fractions import Fraction

def pairs(symbols):
    n = len(symbols)
    matching = sum(c * (c - 1) for c in Counter(symbols).values())
    return matching, n * (n - 1)

def rate(counts):
    matching, total = counts
    return Fraction(matching, total) if total else None

def pooled(symbols, period):
    columns = [pairs(symbols[j::period]) for j in range(period)]
    return rate((sum(a for a, b in columns),
                 sum(b for a, b in columns)))

for text in ("FUFUFFU", "FFUUFFU"):
    print(text, "whole:", rate(pairs(text)), "period 2:", pooled(text, 2))


Expected output:

FUFUFFU whole: 3/7 period 2: 4/9
FFUUFFU whole: 3/7 period 2: 1/3

This example explains an operation, not a tested claim about the manuscript. To apply it, declare the actual rune stream, headings, interruptions, page boundaries, periods and scoring rule first. If you choose the maximum over several periods, each randomized comparison must repeat that same search to evaluate the selected maximum. Comparing the winning period only with a single-period reference would omit the advantage gained by trying many candidates.

Sources and verification

Historical background: William F. Friedman, The Index of Coincidence and Its Applications in Cryptanalysis, preserved by the NSA. The counting convention and derivation used by this script are stated explicitly above; do not assume every historical or modern use of “IoC” has identical scaling.

Inputs: the archived rune files linked by the baseline manifest and their page records. Checks: short examples, exhaustive pair enumeration for three-symbol-alphabet strings of lengths 2–6, reversal and symbol-renaming invariance, and all 75 recorded page counts. These validate the calculation under its declared inputs; they do not independently validate the photographic transcription.

---

What cipher operations preserve

Compare rearrangements, fixed substitutions, and position-dependent shifts before choosing a measurement.

An invariant is something an operation leaves unchanged. In cipher analysis, invariants help you check an implementation and avoid tests that cannot distinguish the candidates you are comparing. If every rearrangement of the same runes has the same whole-stream index of coincidence, selecting the rearrangement with the “best IoC” cannot work.

First fix what counts as a symbol

For the examples here, one symbol is one of the 29 runes, represented by its zero-based index. A label such as TH or NG still represents one rune. Keep the same input boundaries throughout a comparison: removing a heading or dropping punctuation is a preprocessing decision, not part of the substitution or rearrangement itself. See rune indices and prime values and transcription layers.

What each operation preserves

	Measurement	Pure transposition	Fixed one-to-one substitution	Position-dependent shifts

	Number of symbols	Preserved	Preserved	Preserved

	Count of each named rune	Preserved	Not generally preserved	Not generally preserved

	Counts sorted without rune names	Preserved	Preserved	Not guaranteed

	Whole-stream IoC	Preserved	Preserved	Not guaranteed

	Sum of fixed rune prime values	Preserved	Not generally preserved	Not generally preserved

	Which positions contain equal symbols	Not generally preserved	Preserved	Not guaranteed


“Not guaranteed” does not mean “must change.” A particular input can happen to give the same result. A fixed one-to-one substitution uses the same reversible alphabet mapping at every position; ordinary Atbash and a uniform shift are examples. A repeating Vigenère key can instead apply different shifts to different positions.

A five-rune example

Start with F F U F U, or indices 0 0 1 0 1. It has three F runes and two U runes. Its matching-pair numerator is 3 × 2 + 2 × 1 = 8; dividing by 5 × 4 = 20 gives IoC 2/5.

	Operation	Output indices	IoC	What happened

	Reverse the sequence	1 0 1 0 0	2/5	The same runes occupy different positions.

	Add 1 to every index	1 1 2 1 2	2/5	Three F become three U; two U become two TH.

	Subtract the repeating key [0, 1]	0 28 1 28 1	1/5	The counts become 1, 2, and 2 across three runes.


The uniform shift preserves the pattern of repetitions even though it changes the rune names. The first, second, and fourth symbols are still equal. Their prime values are different, however: the original prime sum is 3 × 2 + 2 × 3 = 12, while the uniformly shifted sum is 3 × 3 + 2 × 5 = 19. IoC and a Gematria Primus sum measure different properties.

Why IoC survives alphabet relabeling

The IoC formula uses the counts, not the names attached to them. A reversible substitution merely moves those counts to different alphabet entries. Its numerator and denominator therefore stay the same. A transposition keeps each named count unchanged, so it preserves IoC for an even simpler reason.

This also holds for any statistic calculated only from the multiset of counts, such as empirical symbol entropy. It does not hold for a score that compares named rune frequencies against a particular expected distribution: that score depends on which count belongs to which rune. Nor does it automatically hold for measurements made on selected positions or separate columns, because a rearrangement can move runes across those boundaries.

Reproduce the example

Run this with Python 3. It uses exact fractions and the standard library; no data files, network, or AI calls are needed.

from collections import Counter
from fractions import Fraction

def ioc(symbols):
    n = len(symbols)
    if n < 2:
        return None
    counts = Counter(symbols)
    return Fraction(sum(v * (v - 1) for v in counts.values()), n * (n - 1))

source = [0, 0, 1, 0, 1]
reversed_order = source[::-1]
uniform_shift = [(c + 1) % 29 for c in source]
key = [0, 1]
varying_shift = [(c - key[i % len(key)]) % 29 for i, c in enumerate(source)]

for name, symbols in [
    ("original", source),
    ("reversed", reversed_order),
    ("uniform", uniform_shift),
    ("varying", varying_shift),
]:
    print(name, symbols, ioc(symbols))

assert Counter(source) == Counter(reversed_order)
assert sorted(Counter(source).values()) == sorted(Counter(uniform_shift).values())
assert ioc(source) == ioc(reversed_order) == ioc(uniform_shift) == Fraction(2, 5)
assert ioc(varying_shift) == Fraction(1, 5)

Choose a test that can change

For a transposition search, length and rune counts are integrity checks. To compare candidate orders, examine something sensitive to order, such as repeated neighboring pairs, the distribution within specified columns, or a fully stated language score. A promising score still needs controls for how many arrangements were tried.

For fixed alphabet substitutions, global IoC cannot select the correct mapping. Rune identities and repeated-word patterns can carry information that this single number discards. For position-dependent ciphers, a change in IoC is possible but is not a proof that a key is correct. The IoC guide explains whole-stream versus column measurements; the reproduction guide explains how to record the search scope.

What these checks establish

These are mathematical properties of the operations as defined here, illustrated with an artificial sequence. They are not newly completed experiments on an unsolved page. A proposed transposition that changes the rune counts has done something besides rearranging the fixed input; a proposal that preserves them has passed an integrity check, not proved a solution.

Instars, cicadas and emergence

The biological term, the linked Welcome and Parable passages, and the image beneath LP2-57.

An instar is a developmental stage between molts. Liber Primus uses the term in the Welcome and again in the final parable, connecting inward movement, shedding and emergence. Understanding the biological term makes the comparison more precise without turning the passage into an automatic cipher instruction.

The biological term

The Amateur Entomologists' Society glossary defines an instar as an arthropod's developmental stage between molts. The first instar follows hatching; successive molts lead to later instars. The term applies to insects with both complete and incomplete metamorphosis. It is not a synonym for a cocoon, and it does not name one particular insect species.

In cicadas, a nymph lives underground before emerging and undergoing the final molt into a winged adult. Purdue Extension's account of periodical cicadas describes nymphs leaving the soil, climbing a support and shedding their last shell. Its 13- and 17-year examples concern periodical cicadas; the word “instar” does not itself imply either duration.

Where the manuscript uses it

Keep three things separate while reading: a stage of development, the act of shedding, and the material left behind. The manuscript’s metaphor draws on this general setting, but these biological terms do not name the same thing.

	Passage	Contextual English	Surrounding idea

	LP1-04, Welcome	LIKE THE INSTAR, IT IS ONLY THROUGH GOING WITHIN THAT WE MAY EMERGE	The pilgrimage shapes the self and reality; inward travel leads outward.

	LP2-57, Parable	LIKE THE INSTAR TUNNELING TO THE SURFACE	Shedding circumferences and finding divinity within precede emergence.


These are contextual English renderings. LP1-04's literal labels include LICE-THE-INSTAR and GONG-WITHIN; LP2-57 has LICE-THE-INSTAR-TUNNELNG-TO-THE-SURFACE after joining its line wrap. Keep these literal forms when checking runes or numbers. The contextual wording is not a replacement transcription. See the full Welcome, the full parable and reading conventions.

How the biological terms fit together
Instars are stages; molts separate them
Hatching: the first instar begins.
First instar: a stage of development before the next molt.
Molt: the old outer covering is shed.
Second instar: the next stage begins; later molts separate later instars.
This is a general sequence, not a count of cicada instars or a diagram of the manuscript’s cipher.

Stage, process, and remains

	Term	What it describes	Why the distinction matters here

	Instar	A developmental stage between molts	It is not the empty shell or a species name.

	Ecdysis	The shedding of the old exoskeleton during molting	It names an event rather than the entire intervening stage.

	Exuvia; plural exuviae	The discarded outer covering after a molt	The remains are distinct from the animal that has emerged.


The linked Amateur Entomologists’ Society definitions supply this terminology. Ecdysis and exuvia are explanatory vocabulary introduced here, not additional words decoded from the two cited manuscript passages. Finding a shell-like feature in a drawing would still require visual evidence; this glossary does not classify the LP2-57 figure as an exuvia.

What the repeated image contributes

The repeated term links two distant passages. The Welcome describes going within; the parable makes the movement toward the surface explicit. The parable also connects shedding with “circumferences,” a word used in The Loss of Divinity and the second koan. Together these support a literary interpretation of emergence through the removal of a limiting outer identity.

That interpretation is an analogy, not a biological definition. An insect's exoskeleton and the manuscript's circumference are not interchangeable technical terms. Nor is “going within” a complete description of cicada development. The text selects features of growth and emergence to make a comparison; it does not give an entomological account.

The image beneath the parable

The original LP2-57 image places a black, stippled, winged insect-like figure below the text. Its body runs vertically, with lateral wing shapes and scattered marks around it. Above it are the red heading and enlarged red initial among otherwise black runes. These are observations of the page, not an identification of a species or source illustration.

The adjacent emergence text makes an insect comparison relevant, but it cannot by itself establish what species the drawing represents. A visual attribution would need a matching source image or diagnostic features, with differences recorded. Do not use the surrounding prose as proof that every feature of the drawing is anatomically cicadan. Use the reader's enlarged original to inspect the marks rather than treating a small thumbnail as sufficient evidence.
LP2-57 — stippled figure below the parable. Open reader
Compare other insect drawings in LP2 and the detached wing on LP2-27.
Why the exact spelling still matters

LP2-57's TUNNELNG uses the multi-letter NG/ING rune convention. Inserting a separate I changes the prime sum even if the contextual English looks more familiar. The prime-sum guide reproduces the arithmetic: adding I contributes 31, changing the first body sentence's sum from 1259 to 1290. This is a numerical consequence of a specified alternate encoding, not proof that the author chose the original to achieve that sum.

Likewise, the biology of periodical cicadas does not justify selecting 13 or 17 as a key without a further rule. A test using those numbers needs explicit page scope, transformation, offsets and criteria. A thematic association supplies a candidate, not a result.

Check the connection yourself

Read the complete Welcome and parable, keeping contextual English separate from literal labels.
Compare the instar wording and follow the linked occurrences of circumference.
Inspect the original parable image. Describe visible forms before proposing a species or external source.
Consult the biological definition, then state which part of the manuscript comparison is interpretation.

Sources and status

Manuscript evidence: the linked LP1-04 and LP2-57 records, their preserved source images and known readings, dated to the 5 October 2026 snapshot. Biological references: the AES glossary and Purdue Extension article cited above. Visual description: direct inspection of the preserved LP2-57 JPEG. The literary interpretation does not establish authorial intent, a species attribution or a new decryption. Continue with philosophical themes.


Follow the recurring term in circumference, identity, and emergence, or use the known-reading concordance to locate a word or phrase yourself.

Four unreasonable things and Lewis Carroll

LP1-09 compared with the White Queen: doing versus believing, four versus six, and the limits of the association.

The instruction at the end of Liber Primus's first koan can be compared with the White Queen's impossible-things speech in Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass. The comparison concerns a numbered practice that challenges ordinary expectations. It is a possible literary association, not an established quotation or source attribution.

Compare the actual words

	Source	Wording

	LP1-09, contextual English	DO FOUR UNREASONABLE THINGS EACH DAY

	Carroll, chapter V, “Wool and Water”	Why, sometimes I've believed as many as six impossible things before breakfast.


Carroll's sentence is spoken by the White Queen in Through the Looking-Glass. The primary text at Project Gutenberg places it in a conversation about believing something Alice considers impossible. The Queen treats belief as something improved by practice.

The manuscript's literal sequence, after joining its line wrap, is DO-FOUR-UNREASONABLE-THNGS-EACH-DAY. THINGS is contextual English for THNGS under the rune-label convention. Do not silently replace the literal sequence when investigating its numbers. See transliteration and the complete first koan.

The differences matter

Action: the manuscript says to do things; the Queen describes believing things.
Number: the manuscript gives four; Carroll gives as many as six.
Qualifier: unreasonable is not identical to impossible. An action can be considered unreasonable without being logically or physically impossible.
Time: the manuscript says each day; Carroll's example is before breakfast.
Voice: the manuscript presents a direct instruction, while Carroll gives a character's recollection within a comic dialogue.

Those differences prevent calling the manuscript line a verbatim Carroll quotation. The structural resemblance is worth recording, but it is less specific than the holy-life verbal parallel with Blake. This article does not establish that Carroll was the immediate source of the instruction.

Read the instruction after the story

In LP1-06–09, the master rejects the student's name, occupation, species and description of consciousness as answers to who the student is. Admission to study follows the student's inability to complete another answer. The four-things instruction comes after this exchange, separated as an instruction. A possible reading is that it extends the story's challenge to familiar explanations into a daily exercise. That is editorial interpretation, not an additional decoded message.

Carroll's scene instead concerns Alice's refusal to believe an apparently impossible age and the Queen's response. The two contexts both challenge ordinary judgments, but their immediate questions differ: identity in the koan, belief in the Carroll exchange. A similarity in tone does not demonstrate identical philosophical commitments.

What would make this a cipher hypothesis?

A comparison becomes a testable cipher proposal only when it specifies an operation. “Use Carroll” leaves the text, edition, passage and transformation undetermined. A proposal would need to fix those choices, declare how punctuation and letters become rune indices, and state which manuscript positions consume the key. Record those decisions before inspecting candidate outputs.

The difference between four and six does not itself justify subtracting two from every rune, choosing a six-character key, or treating chapter V as an offset. Each would be a new assumption requiring its own scoped test. Neither the comparison here nor a search result in the wiki counts as evidence that such a technique has been tried. Use Have we tried it? for documented experiment records and the reproducibility guide for their requirements.

How to verify the comparison

Open LP1-09 in the reader, then follow the complete first-koan guide to reproduce the literal reading.
Open Carroll's primary text, locate chapter V and search for “six impossible things.” Read the preceding exchange as well as the famous sentence.
Record both the common structure and the differences listed above. Keep an attribution claim separate from the observable wording.

Sources and status

Manuscript evidence: LP1-09 and the compiled readings, dated to the 5 October 2026 snapshot. External text: Lewis Carroll, Through the Looking-Glass, Gutenberg edition 12, chapter V. Comparison checked on 20 October 2026. The relationship is presented as a possible association, not an authenticated influence. Related: philosophical themes.

https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/transliteration.html
https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/reading-first-koan.html
https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/william-blake.html

The illustrated cover: compasses and Blake artwork

The 1033.jpg collage, its source artworks, original download, and place in the 2014 puzzle.

This is the compasses collage often reproduced as the illustrated cover of Liber Primus. Its archived filename is 1033.jpg. It appeared at an earlier stage of the 2014 puzzle, before the manuscript images catalogued here as LP1 and LP2.
The archived 1033.jpg. Select the image to inspect it at full size.

Download the original JPEG · File provenance and checksum

The artwork in the collage

The image brings together details of William Blake’s works. The repeated compasses are particularly noticeable: the upper panel shows a hand working over a geometrical diagram, while the lower panel shows compasses reaching into darkness.

In his study of the 2014 image, Frank G. Bosman identifies the upper central panel as Newton, the lower central panel as The Ancient of Days, and the two side strips as details of Nebuchadnezzar. These identifications describe the source artworks; they do not by themselves establish what the puzzle authors intended the collage to mean.

For comparison, Tate’s Newton image shows the figure concentrating on a compass and scroll. The British Museum’s catalogue entry for The Ancient of Days describes the figure holding compasses from a heavenly sphere. Cropping and rearrangement matter here: inspect the source compositions before assigning a meaning to a fragment.

Where it appeared in the puzzle

The preceding Self-Reliance book cipher explains how the archived route reached this image.

The archived 2014 walkthrough places this image on the first onion site, auqgnxjtvdbll3pv.onion. The recorded HTML page title is For Every Thing That Lives Is Holy. This gives the collage another connection to Blake, alongside the closely related sentence in the manuscript’s Welcome section. See William Blake and Liber Primus for the wording in context.

The hidden message, reproduced

On 20 October 2026, default-key OutGuess extraction from this exact JPEG recovered 1,498 bytes. The extracted message begins with a greeting, supplies RSA values e and n, and contains an encrypted block labelled Crypt::RSA::ES::OAEP. The clear-signed message verified with GnuPG 2.5.21 against the recorded Cicada public key, using an isolated keyring and no legacy-digest override.

Download the full extraction · Signed message · Read the message body

The three downloads serve different purposes. The extraction preserves every recovered byte. The signed file isolates the PGP block for verification. The body is a readable derivative with PGP framing and dash escaping removed; use the signed file, not this derivative, to check the signature.

How to reproduce the extraction

Extract the reference-data ZIP and original-images ZIP into the same folder. Install OutGuess separately, then run this command from that folder. The wrapper checks the JPEG before extracting and refuses to overwrite an existing output file.

python scripts/extract_payload.py 1033 --outguess outguess --output illustrated-cover.bin

It should report 1,498 verified bytes and this SHA-256:

65ff60bfa019e424ce2ae23994f19af5692f7e12e6bc177830b42a154985defd

If OutGuess is not on your executable search path, replace the second outguess with its full path. See OutGuess extraction for the underlying operation and Running the reproduction scripts for terminal setup.

Next, follow the isolated-keyring instructions to import and check the public key. With that keyring prepared, verify this message:

gpg --no-options --homedir verify-keyring --no-auto-key-retrieve --status-fd 1 --verify exports/steganography/1033.signed.asc

The VALIDSIG line should identify 6D854CD7933322A601C3286D181F01E57A35090F. The evidence record preserves separate hashes, tool identification and the verification status output.

Continue to RSA decryption

Extracting the message does not decrypt the encrypted block. Verifying its signature establishes that the signed text matches the recorded key, not the identity of a person or the authenticity of every pixel in the JPEG. The RSA reproduction guide now recovers the historical next address from all three encrypted blocks, using published factors. It explains the envelope, arithmetic and legacy padding, with a script and recorded outputs.

Why it is separate from page 00

LP1-00 is the plain title page bearing the words Liber Primus. The collage is a different image from an earlier puzzle stage. It therefore has its own entry rather than taking a numbered place in the 75-image manuscript catalogue.

The three-image hidden-message chain uses LP1-00, LP1-01 and LP1-02. Its name can be confusing: that chain concerns the manuscript’s title pages and warning, not this compasses collage. The title-page guide explains those visible headings and hidden messages.

Check the downloaded file

The download preserves the bytes of the JPEG in the pinned community archive; it has not been resized or re-encoded. It is 1327 × 1427 pixels and 342,361 bytes. Matching this checksum confirms the archived file, not who created it.

SHA-256: 15b2b99fe15ff34ef3eab574bb84bfaad0a119674be2ca5baf65951e6a9bd865

The same original is included in the original-images ZIP. Its separate provenance record keeps it distinguishable from the numbered manuscript pages.

Newton: the upper compasses panel

The drawing instrument, Blake’s portrayal of Newton, and how to compare the cover fragment.

The upper central panel of the illustrated cover concentrates on a hand, compasses and a geometrical drawing. Frank G. Bosman’s published identification traces this fragment to William Blake’s Newton. Understanding the whole composition helps explain what the crop leaves out.

What the original depicts

Tate’s reproduction and description show Newton concentrating on a drawing while seated on a textured rock. Tate interprets his attention to the instrument and scroll, and his disregard for his surroundings, as Blake’s criticism of a view of the world confined to rational measurement. This is the museum’s account of Blake’s image, not an explanation supplied by the puzzle authors.

Here, compasses means the hinged drawing instrument used to construct circles and transfer distances. It is not a magnetic compass for finding north. That distinction matters before proposing an operation based on direction, angle or radius.

How to check the fragment

Open the preserved cover JPEG and Tate’s image in separate tabs.
Locate the hand, the two legs of the compasses and the drawing beneath them. Compare their arrangement, rather than matching only the general subject.
Bosman describes the Newton fragment as mirrored. Check left and right against the complete work; record any reflection separately from cropping.
Keep the original JPEG unchanged. If you make an annotated comparison, label it as a derivative and record the source image used.

From artwork to a research question

The other central panel also contains compasses: see The Ancient of Days. Their repetition makes measurement a reasonable subject for interpretation. It does not specify a numerical cipher. A test based on the drawing would still need to say which points are measured, how image scaling is handled, and how a measurement becomes a symbol.

For the manuscript’s own language about perception and the individual, follow philosophical themes. The Blake overview treats the separate verbal parallel in Welcome.

Nebuchadnezzar: the cover’s side panels

The biblical figure in Blake’s artwork and the distinction between identification and a proposed book source.

The narrow strips beside the central compasses panels are identified as fragments of William Blake’s Nebuchadnezzar in Frank G. Bosman’s study of the cover. They are easy to overlook because the collage splits the composition into its margins.

Who is Nebuchadnezzar?

In Tate’s account of Blake’s work, the subject is the biblical king reduced to an animal-like existence as punishment for pride. Tate dates its work to 1795–about 1805 and identifies the medium as colour print with ink and watercolour on paper. The title names the figure in the artwork; it is not a word transcribed from the cover.

How to inspect the side panels

Begin with the unchanged cover image and the full composition shown by Tate. Follow the outlines of the limbs and hair through each narrow strip. Bosman describes rotated fragments; compare orientation as well as shape. A fragment can become difficult to recognize when a familiar horizontal body is turned into a vertical border.

Record which source reproduction you compare. Different photographs and impressions can differ in colour, contrast and framing. Identifying the composition is a different task from identifying the exact digital image used to assemble the collage.

Why the Book of Daniel enters the discussion

The book-cipher guide explains what must be specified before a proposed book source becomes a reproducible lookup.

Bosman develops a proposed Daniel connection from the cover’s imagery. That is an interpretive argument, not a reproduced book-cipher result. Recognizing Nebuchadnezzar explains why someone might investigate a biblical source; it does not select a passage, translation or indexing rule.

If you pursue that idea, the experiment-writing guide explains how to state those choices before testing. Keep the artwork identification and the proposed cipher test as separate claims so another reader can accept one without being asked to accept the other.

Return to the cover overview, or compare the central panels: Newton and The Ancient of Days.

The Ancient of Days: the lower compasses panel

The frontispiece, the figure with compasses, and why the exact Blake copy matters.

The lower central panel of the compasses cover is identified as a detail of William Blake’s The Ancient of Days by Frank G. Bosman’s cover study. The complete composition supplies context that is lost when the hand and instrument are isolated.

What is a frontispiece?

A frontispiece is an illustration placed at the beginning of a book. The British Museum’s record for Europe: a Prophecy, copy A, plate 1 identifies this design as its frontispiece. The catalogue describes a bearded figure in a luminous sphere, extending compasses into the darkness below. It gives the figure’s identity as probably Urizen; that qualification should remain when citing the record.

The collection record describes a particular copy. A work title alone does not identify which impression, colouring or modern reproduction was used in the puzzle image. This entry does not establish that the collage was made from the museum’s copy A.

How to compare the cover

Open the original cover and the museum’s complete design.
Trace the hand and the two legs of the instrument. Compare their relationship to the surrounding light and the partly visible head.
Check the orientation: Bosman describes a rotated fragment. Record the rotation and crop separately instead of treating a transformed image as a different drawing.
To identify an exact source copy, compare small distinctive details and colour placement across documented copies, not merely the common outline.

What the repeated instrument tells us

Newton, in the upper panel, also supplies a hand with compasses. The collage therefore places two acts of measurement together. Reading that arrangement as a theme is different from extracting a key from it: a cipher proposal needs an explicit rule that someone else can apply to the same source bytes.

See Nebuchadnezzar for the side panels and the proposed Daniel connection, and William Blake and Liber Primus for the manuscript’s textual allusion.

Decrypting the illustrated cover’s RSA message

Reproduce the three historical RSA blocks and understand the Crypt::RSA 1.99 padding difference.

The 1033.jpg cover hides a signed message containing an RSA public key and encrypted data. This guide reproduces the historical decryption using published factors. It recovers a navigation address from the 2014 puzzle; it does not solve an unknown manuscript page.

Run the reproduction

Extract the reference-data ZIP. From the extracted folder, run:

python scripts/reproduce_cover_rsa.py

The script needs only Python 3’s standard library. It reads the included verified message body and makes no network requests. Its output lists three blocks, their recovered bytes and successful RSA round-trip checks. The complete plaintext is:

\ncu343l33nqaekrnw.onion\n\n

Here \n denotes a newline byte. The address is historical output, not a service contacted by this reproduction. Download the recorded result or inspect the script.

What the key numbers mean

The signed body gives e = 65537 and a modulus n. The modulus is the integer that defines the range of RSA arithmetic; this one is 432 bits long. The public exponent e specifies the public modular-power operation. To undo it, this reproduction uses two published factors, p and q, whose product equals n.

Connor Tumbleson’s reconstruction supplies those factors. The script checks their product against the modulus read from the message, calculates phi = (p - 1)(q - 1), and obtains the private exponent as the modular inverse d = e⁻¹ mod phi. Supplying the factors avoids repeating factor discovery. The fast runtime of this script therefore says nothing about how long factoring took.

Unwrap the message in the right order

Base64: decode the printable encrypted block into bytes.
Checksum: compare the attached MD5 value with the compressed bytes. This is the historical format’s integrity check, not a substitute for the PGP signature.
Compression: decompress the zlib stream.
Content frame: read the length-prefixed field named Cyphertext, preserving that spelling. It holds 162 bytes: three 54-byte RSA blocks.
RSA: for each ciphertext integer c, calculate m = cᵈ mod n. Re-encrypt m and require the original c.
Padding: decode the legacy OAEP structure and concatenate the three recovered message fragments.

Why an ordinary OAEP decoder can fail

OAEP adds structured padding before RSA encryption. Recovering the modular integer is only part of decryption; the padding must also be decoded using the same rules as the sender.

The message names Crypt::RSA::ES::OAEP, version 1.99. In that release’s DataFormat.pm, the SHA-1 mask generator uses counters 0, 20, 40 and so on. Standard MGF1 advances by one instead. This small implementation difference changes the mask bytes and causes a standard decoder to reject this message’s padding. The reproduction follows the named legacy implementation and checks the empty-label hash and padding delimiter in every block.

On 20 October 2026, a separate PyCryptodome 3.23.0 OAEP decoder with the legacy mask rule matched all three fragments. Its default mask rejected all three. This is a compatibility finding about this historical message, not a reason to use these old rules for new encryption.

Sources and scope

Input: the extracted message body, with its hash checked before decoding. Signature and extraction evidence: cover provenance. Implementation reference: Crypt::RSA 1.99 source archive, especially DataFormat.pm and ES/OAEP.pm. The result record includes the archive checksum and block-level outputs.

The complete path is now OutGuess extraction, signature verification, then this RSA replay. These operations establish different things: recovered carrier bytes, a valid signed message, and a matching historical plaintext.

https://jelliottdev.github.io/scripts/reproduce_cover_rsa.py

Emerson’s Self-Reliance and the opening book cipher

The essay’s documented place in the 2014 route, a first-coordinate example, and comparisons with Liber Primus.

Ralph Waldo Emerson’s Self-Reliance belongs in the history of the 2014 puzzle for a specific reason: the archived opening route uses it as a book-cipher source. It also offers useful comparisons with Liber Primus’s treatment of inward knowledge and conformity. Those are two different connections, with different kinds of evidence.

Its place before the illustrated cover

The pinned 2014 walkthrough identifies Emerson’s essay as the source indicated by the opening riddle. It records a four-part lookup rule: paragraph, sentence, word, letter. The reported result is auqgnxjtvdbll3pv.onion, the historical site that displayed the 1033.jpg compasses collage.

This places the essay before the cover’s RSA message. The two addresses belong to successive steps; they are not conflicting solutions to the same clue. Neither address is contacted by the site’s reproduction scripts.

Follow the first coordinate

The walkthrough points to this Dartmouth-hosted PDF of Self-Reliance. The first coordinate is 1:2:3:1. Count from the first prose paragraph, after the title and opening verse. Its second sentence begins The soul always. The third word is always, whose first letter is a. This agrees with the first character of the reported address.

Reproduce all the lookups

The complete replay was checked on 20 October 2026. Extract the reference-data ZIP and run:

python scripts/reproduce_emerson.py

This uses Python’s standard library and the included paragraph derivative. It prints the complete result and every selected sentence, word and character. The output is auqgnxjtvdbll3pv.onion; no network request is made.

For a second level of reproduction, install pypdf==6.19.0 in your Python environment and run python scripts/reproduce_emerson.py --check-pdf. This re-extracts the included source PDF and compares all 50 derived paragraphs before doing the lookups. The default command does not require that package.

	Coordinate or literal	Selected word	Character
	1:2:3:1	always	a
	3:3:13:5	genius	u
	45:5:2:3	acquires	q
	20:3:20:5	among	g
	8:3:8:6	action	n
	48:5:14:2	experience	x
	21:13:4:1	justice	j
	25:1:7:4	truth	t
	15:9:3:4	above	v
	1:1:16:3	and	d
	4:3:3:1	being	b
	8:3:26:4	daily	l
	47:3:3:5	equality	l
	3	Printed literally	3
	13:2:5:4	corpse	p
	1:4:16:4	private	v
	.	Printed literally	.
	o	Printed literally	o
	n	Printed literally	n
	i	Printed literally	i
	o	Printed literally	o
	n	Printed literally	n

The counting rules used here

Counting starts at the first prose paragraph and excludes the title, opening verse and page-number footers. Sentences end at periods, question marks or exclamation marks. Words are separated by whitespace, with punctuation removed from their edges; only alphabetic characters count within the selected word. All coordinates start at 1. Typographical ligatures are expanded, and words split with a line-ending hyphen are joined while retaining the hyphen.

One detail changes the later paragraph numbers: the two inset verse lines on printed page 16 stay within paragraph 36. They are not two additional prose paragraphs. An initial automatic extraction counted them separately; inspecting the PDF explained the resulting mismatches. This is a documented correction during replay of a known result, not an independently predicted decoding rule.

The full evidence record contains source and derivative checksums, every coordinate and selected sentence, and the conventions. The paragraph derivative records the printed starting page for each paragraph. The coordinates are now read directly from the freshly extracted and signature-verified opening message. The script checks the body checksum and coordinate sequence before replaying them. It also does not establish that the PDF snapshot is byte-for-byte the edition originally used by the puzzle authors.

What “self-reliance” means in the essay

Read the essay in Emerson’s Essays, First Series, under Self-Reliance. Emerson’s instruction to Trust thyself concerns confidence in one’s own judgment rather than dependence on social approval. His argument against conformity questions obedience to inherited opinion. These are claims about how to think and live, not a set of cipher instructions.

There are useful points of comparison with Liber Primus’s final LP1 instruction, which directs attention inward, and The Loss of Divinity, which examines adherence and the desire to belong. Read the passages together before calling them equivalent: the manuscript develops its own vocabulary of circumference, divinity and primality.

There is also a tension worth keeping visible. Emerson’s appeal to self-trust does not automatically explain the manuscript’s promised end to self or its koans about identity. The same word can carry different meanings in different arguments. The philosophical themes guide follows those distinctions within Liber Primus.

Three passages to read closely

The locations below use the same 50-paragraph source derivative as the reproduction script. Paragraphs count from one. The printed page is where the paragraph starts in the preserved Dartmouth PDF; these numbers should not be transferred to another edition.

Conformity: paragraph 6, printed page 3

“The virtue in most request is conformity. Self-reliance is its aversion.”

The surrounding passage compares society to a company whose members exchange some independence for security. Emerson’s objection concerns the price of acceptance: a person may surrender judgment to inherited names and customs. This is more specific than a general instruction to be different.

Compare The Loss of Divinity, where adherence is criticized when its motive is belonging and being right. The manuscript explicitly includes both dogma and reason as things a person might follow for that motive. The overlap is a concern about dependence on approval; the wording and surrounding explanations are not identical.

Consistency: paragraph 14, printed page 7

“Speak what you think now in hard words, and to-morrow speak what to-morrow thinks in hard words again, though it contradict every thing you said to-day.”

This follows Emerson’s famous criticism of a “foolish consistency.” The practical issue is whether loyalty to an earlier statement prevents a person from expressing a present conviction. Read the paragraph rather than reducing the phrase to permission for arbitrary contradiction.

Liber Primus’s warning directs readers to test knowledge, while also preserving the book’s words and numbers. Those instructions address different objects: a reader’s beliefs may change while the source being examined remains intact. That is an internal comparison with the manuscript, not evidence that this particular Emerson paragraph supplied its wording.

Fortune and inward stability: paragraph 50, printed page 21

“Nothing can bring you peace but yourself. Nothing can bring you peace but the triumph of principles.”

In the preceding sentences, Emerson lists favorable events that can raise someone’s spirits, including a political victory and the return of an absent friend. His conclusion shifts attention from those changing circumstances to the self and principles. It is an argument about where stability is sought, not a claim that outward events never matter.

The manuscript’s discussion of possessions and fear of losing them offers a useful comparison: The Loss of Divinity distinguishes accumulating wealth from attachment to it. Yet Emerson’s concluding self-trust and Liber Primus’s promised end to self should not be flattened into a single teaching. The koans ask what identity means; they do not merely repeat an instruction to trust an already-defined self.

Keep the historical and interpretive claims distinct

	Claim	Evidence available here

	The essay functions as a source in the opening book cipher.	The preserved coordinates, declared counting rules, and reproduced historical output.

	Its arguments can be compared with Liber Primus.	The passages above beside the documented manuscript readings.

	A specific passage intentionally inspired a manuscript sentence.	Not established by thematic resemblance or the book-cipher replay alone.

	The essay provides a key for another page.	Requires a separately specified and tested transformation.


This lets the essay play two useful roles without confusing them: a concrete input in a historical computation, and a text to read alongside the manuscript’s ideas.

A reading edition is not automatically a cipher edition

The Gutenberg text is useful for reading the essay and locating themes. The Dartmouth PDF is the edition linked by the walkthrough. Do not assume that paragraph, sentence or word counts can be transferred between them without comparison. A line break introduced by a PDF page boundary is not necessarily a paragraph break; titles, epigraphs and footnotes can also shift a naïve count.

The historical use of this essay makes it a documented source in the earlier puzzle. It does not establish that Emerson supplies a key to an unsolved LP2 page. Any such proposal needs its own input, selection rule and reproducible test.

Book ciphers: coordinates, editions and counting rules

How text lookups work and what to preserve so another reader can reproduce them.

A book cipher turns coordinates into text by looking them up in a shared source. The source can be an essay, poem or other document; it need not be a whole book. To reproduce a result, knowing the title is not enough. You also need the edition and the rules used to count its parts.

How a four-part lookup works

In a paragraph:sentence:word:letter scheme, 2:1:3:2 means: select paragraph 2, then its first sentence, then its third word, then the second letter of that word. This assumes one-based counting, where the first item is numbered 1.

For a small invented example, let paragraph 2 begin We study runes. The third word is runes, so the second letter is u. The coordinates identify nested locations; they are not numbers to add together.

The archived 2014 opening puzzle uses this kind of rule with Emerson’s Self-Reliance. That guide traces all 15 coordinates and the literal characters against a derivative of the referenced PDF, with downloadable source files and a reproduction script.

Decide what counts before extracting
Starting pointState whether titles, opening quotations and notes are included. Starting at the first prose paragraph can differ from starting at the first text on the page.
Paragraph boundariesPreserve actual paragraph divisions. A page or display line ending may interrupt a paragraph without creating a new one.
Sentence boundariesSpecify how punctuation and abbreviations are handled. Splitting blindly at every period can create false sentences.
Word and letter boundariesRecord how hyphens, apostrophes, punctuation and accented letters are treated. Counting characters in a raw file is not necessarily counting letters in the printed word.
Literal charactersA clue may print some digits or punctuation directly. Identify those separately instead of forcing every item through the coordinate rule.

What a reproducible trace should show

For each coordinate, record the selected paragraph, sentence, word and letter, plus the resulting output character. Include the source URL, a file checksum, and any transcription changes. A reader should be able to inspect one disagreeing character without rerunning an opaque decoder.

If a coordinate points beyond a sentence or word, report it as out of range. Wrapping around, skipping a heading or switching editions introduces another rule. Such a rule may be worth testing, but it must be stated rather than hidden inside a correction.

Using a possible literary reference

A recognizable quotation or artwork can suggest a source to investigate. It does not identify the indexing scheme. Before trying many passages and counting conventions, write down the source, coordinates, transformations and success criterion. Otherwise a promising fragment may simply be the best-looking result among many undocumented choices.

The experiment-writing guide explains how to preserve that scope. Use Have we tried it? to look for a documented test of the same technique and inputs, rather than treating any mention of the source as evidence that the test was performed.

Sources, related references, and files
https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/emerson-self-reliance.html
https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/reproducibility.html
https://jelliottdev.github.io/#/experiments

The 2014 opening image and its hidden message

The original zN4h51m.jpg, verified OutGuess content, and the route through Emerson to the compasses cover.

The opening image of the archived 2014 route is a dark JPEG with a greeting, a pilgrimage announcement, a faint insect-like figure and the number 3301. Its archive filename is zN4h51m.jpg. Unlike a numbered Liber Primus page, its role here is to introduce the route that leads to the manuscript.
The unchanged opening JPEG. The faint central image is part of the source, not a loading error.

Download the original JPEG · Provenance and verification evidence

The visible image and hidden message

The visible text announces the beginning of a journey. The hidden OutGuess message supplies something operational: a short riddle, fifteen four-part coordinates, and several literal characters. The Self-Reliance guide shows how those coordinates select letters from Emerson’s essay.

The extraction was reproduced on 20 October 2026 and recovered exactly 1,150 bytes. The clear-signed block verified with GnuPG 2.5.21 against the recorded Cicada fingerprint, in an isolated keyring without a digest-policy override. Signature verification authenticates the signed message against that key; it does not sign the entire JPEG or establish a real-world author.

Full extraction · Signed block · Readable body

Reproduce the extraction and lookup

Extract the reference data and original images into the same folder. With OutGuess installed, run:

python scripts/extract_payload.py opening-2014 --outguess outguess --output opening.bin

The wrapper checks the input JPEG and the recovered output before writing a new file. Expected output: 1,150 bytes with SHA-256 cba64781bd461b17039316ef97426f912aae987fde131f62e883f7f9e9f0118e. It refuses to overwrite an existing file.

Prepare the isolated keyring using the signature guide, then verify the preserved block:

gpg --no-options --homedir verify-keyring --no-auto-key-retrieve --status-fd 1 --verify exports/steganography/opening-2014.signed.asc

The expected VALIDSIG fingerprint is 6D854CD7933322A601C3286D181F01E57A35090F. Next run python scripts/reproduce_emerson.py. That script reads the coordinates from the extracted body, checks its checksum and reproduces every lookup. It does not invoke GnuPG itself.

How the early steps connect

This opening image carries the riddle and coordinates.
The Emerson book cipher yields the historical address where the compasses collage appeared.
The collage contains a different signed message, with RSA parameters and encrypted bytes.
The RSA replay recovers the next historical address using published factors.

These are earlier puzzle artifacts, separate from the 75 numbered manuscript records. The source image is preserved from the pinned community archive; the same archive’s walkthrough documents the route. Reproducing it does not require visiting the historical services.

The two koans: identity and the inner voice

A close reading of the master–student exchanges, their use of circumference, and the limits of a Zen attribution.

Liber Primus labels two sections A Koan. Both stage an exchange between a master and a student, but they ask different questions. The first tests the descriptions a person offers as an identity. The second turns a denial of an inner voice into an example of that voice.

Read the first section, LP1-06–09, and the second section, LP1-14–15, alongside this guide. Their pages, literal readings and decoding instructions are separate from the interpretation offered here.

What is a koan?

In Zen contexts, a kōan can take the form of a puzzling question or encounter used in training. It is not simply a brainteaser whose purpose is to produce a clever verbal answer. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy’s account of Japanese Zen, section 2, places kōan practice within cultivation of wisdom and compassion, and describes its particular role in Rinzai training.

That background helps explain why a master might reject an answer that is factually correct. It does not identify Liber Primus’s dialogues with any particular traditional case. The manuscript gives the genre label but supplies no author, collection, case number or lineage for either story.

First koan: what an answer describes

The first student seeks admission to study. Each answer to the master’s identity question changes the kind of description being offered:

	Answer offered	How the master classifies it	What changes in the exchange

	A name	A label used to address the person	The question is separated from naming.

	A profession	An activity or social role	The question is separated from work.

	Being human	Membership in a species	The answer moves from social identity to a biological category.

	Consciousness inhabiting a body	An account of what the person is	Even an abstract account does not satisfy the master’s distinction.


The student eventually begins an answer and cannot complete it. After the pause, the master admits him. The story ends with admission rather than a final definition of the self. One reading is that the student has reached the limits of the descriptions he initially relied on. Another emphasis would be his change from confident answers to uncertainty. Neither reading requires supplying a missing final word as if it were decoded plaintext.

The instruction that follows the exchange is a separate textual feature. Its comparison with Lewis Carroll is discussed in the Carroll guide; a possible connection there does not identify the source of the preceding dialogue.

Second koan: the denial becomes the example

The second master associates the “I” with the voice of the circumference. A student inwardly denies having such a voice and prepares to object. The master points to the just-formed denial as the example the student was looking for.

The exchange is self-referential: an act of thinking about thought becomes part of the argument. Its effect depends on the narration telling us what this student thought. The story does not establish that every person experiences thought as verbal inner speech, nor does it offer a psychological test of readers.

Its vocabulary also belongs to the surrounding manuscript. The Loss of Divinity assigns consumption, preservation and adherence to the circumference. LP2-57’s parable describes shedding circumferences. Following those uses gives the term more context than treating it immediately as a reference to circles in a diagram.

How the two stories work together

The first dialogue unsettles what the student can say about himself; the second questions the voice doing the saying. This is a useful internal connection between the stories. It also helps frame the Welcome section’s promised end to self: what is being brought to an end—a person, a description, or a habitual way of identifying oneself? The manuscript’s stories make that question available without settling it through a formal definition.

Compare Emerson’s self-trust with care. The earlier puzzle’s use of Emerson is documented, but “self” need not mean the same thing in every work. Likewise, identifying the stories as koans does not establish that every claim in Liber Primus belongs to Zen doctrine.

What would establish an outside source?

A source claim needs a specific passage, a traceable edition or translation, and enough shared wording or structure to compare the exchanges in detail. A generic master-and-student story is weak evidence by itself. If a candidate is found, record differences as well as similarities and ask whether the source predates the manuscript.

Keep a literary interpretation separate from a cipher proposal. If “circumference” suggests a key or a reading path, state the exact symbols and transformation, then follow the reproduction requirements. A thematic connection is a reason to investigate; the resulting computation still needs to be checked.

Sources and reading status

The analysis above uses the first koan and second koan in the 5 October 2026 reading snapshot. The Zen reference supplies background, not an attribution of the manuscript. For the wider internal connections, continue with philosophical themes.


Follow the recurring term in circumference, identity, and emergence, or use the known-reading concordance to locate a word or phrase yourself.

Dots and punctuation

Find five-dot arrangements on LP2-07 and LP2-23, three-dot rows on LP2-33 and LP2-39, and small punctuation clusters.

“Dots” can mean several visibly different things in Liber Primus. Large dots separated by wide spaces, small marks between runes, and compact multi-dot clusters should not be treated as one symbol just because a transcription uses similar punctuation for them.
Five large dots on LP2-07 and LP2-23
LP2-07 has five large black dots beneath its red closing line. They form a loose arrangement rather than one straight row. Smaller specks also appear beside the upper spiral drawings, so “the dots on page 7” should specify which group is meant.LP2-07 · Read
See spirals and branching borders for the surrounding LP2-03–07 group.
LP2-23 also has five large dots, this time above the text. Their placement differs from the group below the text on LP2-07. A relationship between these arrangements would need a specified comparison; the shared count alone does not establish a code.LP2-23 — five large dots above the text. Open reader
Continue with the Mayfly group and insect imagery.
Large separated dots
LP2-33 has three conspicuous black dots between two blocks of text. LP2-39 also has a separated row of three dots. These are useful starting points when someone remembers “the page with dots.” This pair is a set of illustrated examples, not an exhaustive dot inventory of all 75 pages.Three large separated dots between the text blocks on LP2-33. Page record · Original JPEGThree separated dots within the layout of LP2-39. Page record · Original JPEG
Small marks and compact clusters
The LP2-00–02 inventory records punctuation separately from rune shapes. Its measured regions include one-, four-, and thirteen-component groups. A “component” is a connected set of dark pixels under a specified threshold. It is not automatically one intentional dot: touching marks can merge, and tiny specks can be excluded.Published measurements for the opening pages
	Page	Punctuation regions	Recorded groups	Red punctuation
	LP2-00	58	56 × one; 1 × four; 1 × thirteen	One one-component region and the thirteen-component region
	LP2-01	62	57 × one; 5 × four	None under the recorded rule
	LP2-02	38	36 × one; 1 × four; 1 × thirteen	The thirteen-component region
The printed mark and the exported character
In the archive notation, a comma represents a three-dot symbol; a period is a clause separator, and an ampersand is a paragraph separator. These are editorial conventions. They are not instructions to insert the prime value of a comma, reset a key, or skip a rune.
One exported character can stand for visually different marks. Before a punctuation-based experiment, identify the exact image regions and the precise sequence you are testing. Otherwise a result may describe the transcriber’s decisions rather than the printed manuscript.
Inspect and reproduce
Open an opening-page record and expand “Recorded punctuation regions.”
Use “Inspect region” to compare the stored rectangle against the full image.
Follow the opening-page reproduction instructions to rerun the pixel counts.
For the measurement rules, see image regions and connected components. For archived versus reviewed punctuation, see the punctuation review record. The large-dot examples above have not been assigned a cipher function.
Related visual features
The repeated cuneiform-like mark · Möbius and the crossed loop · Illustrated index

For red headings, numbers, and marks, see rubrication and color boundaries, with illustrated examples and guidance for recording a proposed extraction.

Möbius and the crossed-loop drawing

Find the LP2-15–22 grouping, inspect the loop beneath the number panel, and distinguish the visual name from a geometric claim.

The name Möbius (also written Mobius or Moebius) is used for the LP2-15–22 section. The most recognizable detail is the crossed, two-lobed drawing beneath the numbers on LP2-15. Start there if you remember an infinity-shaped symbol or a number square.LP2-15: the number panel, crossed loop, and runic text on the complete original sheet. Page record · Original JPEG
What the drawing shows
The two lobes cross, but their outlines have visible openings. The recorded inspection describes an open-loop drawing. “Infinity sign” is a useful way to find it; it does not establish an exact Unicode symbol or a number encoded by that symbol.
A Möbius strip is a surface made by joining the ends of a strip with a half-twist. An infinity sign is a two-dimensional figure-eight shape. Those are different objects: a crossed outline alone cannot demonstrate that a surface has a half-twist. A proposed Möbius interpretation needs to specify how the page’s lines, crossings, and gaps encode that surface.
Pages in the community grouping
The grouping runs from LP2-15 through LP2-22. It does not mean that every sheet contains the same motif, or that all eight use the same cipher. Select any preview to inspect that page’s record.LP2-15 · ReadLP2-16 · ReadLP2-17 · ReadLP2-18 · ReadLP2-19 · ReadLP2-20 · ReadLP2-21 · ReadLP2-22 · Read
Following the numerical details
The panel contains sixteen numbers; 3299 is red. The panel article gives every value, row and column totals, and a reproducible calculation. For an idea involving prime positions or reversed digits, use prime indices and emirps before assigning those operations to the drawing.
There is also a literal MOBIUS in the known Some Wisdom reading. That textual occurrence is a separate piece of evidence. A shared name is a reason to compare the pages, not proof that one supplies a key for the other.
Sources and further reading
Cicada Solvers’ LP2 index supplies the community section names and ranges. The page links above provide original images, checksums, and pinned archive sources. Section names are descriptive navigation labels, not decrypted headings.
Return to the illustrated index to compare other manuscript motifs.

---

Cuneiform-like mark

Compare the repeated mark on LP2-33–39, including its different placement on the first page.

A compact, two-row mark repeats on LP2-33–39. It is commonly called the cuneiform mark. The visible mark belongs in an illustrated index even though its intended meaning is not established.LP2-33: the mark appears below the runic text, near the foot of the page. Page record · Original JPEGLP2-34: the repeated mark appears above the runic text. Page record · Original JPEG
Where to find it
Placement matters. On LP2-33 the mark is at the bottom; on LP2-34–39 it is above the main text. Calling it a “header” without that exception would hide a potentially relevant layout difference. The previews below let you compare all seven sheets.LP2-33 · ReadLP2-34 · ReadLP2-35 · ReadLP2-36 · ReadLP2-37 · ReadLP2-38 · ReadLP2-39 · Read
What the name tells us
The British Museum’s Mesopotamia guide explains how early pictograms developed into wedge-shaped writing called cuneiform. Here it is the community’s name for a visual resemblance. Identifying the manuscript mark as a particular historical sign would require a sign-by-sign comparison with a specified script, period, orientation, and reading. The label alone is not a translation.
The repeated motif is also not part of the ordinary 29-rune Gematria Primus alphabet. Do not assign it a rune index or prime value merely because it occurs beside runic text.
Other details in this section
LP2-33 and LP2-39 show conspicuous separated black dots. LP2-36–38 include red decimal labels: 1 on page 36, 2–4 on page 37, and 5 on page 38. These observations help locate parts of the section; they do not establish what a dot or label instructs the reader to do. See dots and punctuation for the distinction between printed shapes and transcription notation.
How to compare repeated marks
Download the original JPEGs from the page records.
Record a rectangle around each mark in original-image pixels. Include enough surrounding whitespace to preserve orientation.
Compare both appearance and placement. Scaling a preview for display is not evidence that the source marks have identical dimensions.
If testing pixel equality, state the alignment, scale, threshold, and compression tolerance. Visual similarity alone does not establish identical bytes.
The image-region guide explains coordinate and threshold conventions. This article records location and appearance; it does not claim a completed pixel-equality test or a decipherment.
Sources

For red headings, numbers, and marks, see rubrication and color boundaries, with illustrated examples and guidance for recording a proposed extraction.

---

Spirals and branching borders

Compare the curled borders on LP2-03–07 with the branching designs on LP2-40–55, and plan a measurable geometric comparison.

Several groups of Liber Primus pages have curled drawings beside the text. The community calls LP2-03–07 “Spirals,” LP2-40–53 “Spiral Branches,” and LP2-54–55 “Spiral & Dead Tree.” These names make the images easier to find. Comparing their actual linework is more useful than treating every curl as the same symbol.
The curled borders on LP2-03–07
On LP2-03, paired curves frame the left and right margins of the runic text. Each side has a tighter upper curl and a longer lower curve. LP2-07 retains this border arrangement, while its lower text ends above a red line and five large black dots.LP2-03 · ReadLP2-07 · Read
The dots are a separate feature from the small groups of specks beside the upper curls. See dots and punctuation for examples of why position, size, and arrangement should be recorded separately.
Open the intervening pages: LP2-04 · LP2-05 · LP2-06.
The branching borders on LP2-40–55
LP2-40 has curls joined to branching, root-like forms on both sides of the text. LP2-53 shows a winged insect below its red closing passage. The next pair, LP2-54–55, continues the branching border style; LP2-55 also contains a pale tree-shaped drawing above a winged insect.LP2-40 · ReadLP2-53 · ReadLP2-54 · ReadLP2-55 · Read
Use the illustrated index to inspect the intervening LP2-40–53 pages. The branches and trees article compares these forms with the narrow branching drawing on LP2-08–14.
A useful comparison starts with a question
	Question	What to record	What the result would establish
	Do two pages reuse the same border?	Original-file hashes, crop rectangles, alignment, and pixel differences	Agreement under the stated alignment and tolerance
	Are the two margins mirror images?	A defined reflection axis and corresponding points on both drawings	How closely the selected regions match after reflection
	Does a curl follow a particular spiral?	A centre, sampled points, coordinate scale, fitted parameters, and residuals	The quality of that geometric fit, compared with alternatives
For example, a logarithmic spiral has r = a exp(bθ), while an Archimedean spiral has r = a + bθ. Here r is distance from the chosen centre and θ is angle. Merely seeing a curl does not select either model. The chosen centre and the thickness of the drawn line can strongly affect a fit.
Before connecting geometry to a cipher, state how a measured result would change the decoding operation. “The borders look symmetric” and “read alternate lines backwards” are separate claims; the first does not supply the second without an explicit rule.
Preparing a reproducible image comparison
Choose the pages and the feature before fitting anything. Include a comparison page with a visibly different border.
Download the original files and verify their SHA-256 hashes.
Record rectangles using original-image coordinates. Keep the original pixels and any transformed comparison image separately.
Document scaling, rotation, reflection, thresholding, and the score used to compare the shapes.
Publish the script and output together, including mismatches. A visually plausible overlay alone is not enough to reproduce the comparison.
This article provides an inspection route and a comparison method. It does not report a completed geometric fit or establish a cipher role for the borders.
Sources
