Branches and trees

Locate the narrow branching drawings on LP2-08–14 and the pale tree on LP2-55; distinguish tips, junctions, and segments before counting.

Branching forms occur in several parts of LP2. They differ in placement and appearance: a narrow drawing beside the text on LP2-08–14, curled borders later in the manuscript, and a pale tree-shaped drawing inside LP2-55. Keeping these examples separate makes it possible to compare them without losing their page context.
The narrow branching drawing on LP2-08–14
LP2-08 shows a long, slender form along the left margin. Smaller lines branch off toward its upper and lower ends, while the main text sits to its right. LP2-14 shows the same broad arrangement and includes an insect drawing below the text at the right.LP2-08 · ReadLP2-14 · Read
The community groups LP2-08–14 under “Branches.” Open the middle pages to compare placement and linework: 09 · 10 · 11 · 12 · 13. The group name does not establish that the form represents a particular plant species, diagram, or cipher key.
Curled borders and the pale tree
On LP2-40, branching forms are part of the curled drawings on both sides of the text. LP2-55 has that border style as well as a much lighter tree-shaped drawing in the central space above the insect. Its low contrast is itself a reason to consult the original image rather than relying on a transcription.LP2-40 · ReadLP2-55 · Read
Compare the spiral and branching borders, or use the illustrated index to browse the other artwork groups, including the separately named LP2-27–32 “Wing & Tree” group.
The Wing and Tree group adds another distinct example: the soft-edged tree-shaped figure on LP2-32. It should not be conflated with the pale, more finely outlined drawing on LP2-55.LP2-32 — soft-edged tree-shaped drawing. Open reader
What does “count the branches” mean?
A branch count sounds straightforward until two people trace the same drawing differently. One may count every visible line leaving a trunk; another may count terminal tips; a third may count each segment between junctions. Those are different measurements.
	Quantity	A possible explicit definition
	Tips	Endpoints of a traced line, excluding the boundary of the chosen crop
	Junctions	Locations where three or more traced segments meet
	Segments	Paths between tips or junctions, with no junction in their interior
	Main stem	A selected path identified by its endpoints and a stated selection rule
Under a graph representation, tips and junctions become vertices and the connecting segments become edges. A visually tree-like drawing need not yield a mathematical tree: a crossing may or may not be a connection, and a closed loop would change the graph. Publish an annotated tracing so another person can see those choices.
Handling the pale drawing on LP2-55
Increasing contrast can make a faint line easier to see, but it also changes the displayed pixels. Preserve the original file, label an enhanced image as a derivative, and record the operation. If a claim depends on a feature visible only after enhancement, show the corresponding unmodified region too.
For numerical work, choose the brightness threshold before counting and check how modest changes affect the result. A count that changes sharply with the threshold needs that sensitivity reported. The existing image-region guide explains thresholds used for other published measurements; those settings have not been validated as a segmentation method for this pale tree.
From appearance to interpretation
A botanical identification, a religious association, and a decoding instruction each require different evidence. A comparison with a named artwork should show the proposed source image and the matching features. A cipher proposal should specify how the drawing produces an ordered sequence or operation, rather than selecting a count because it happens to fit.
For wider interpretation, start with philosophical themes in the known readings. That article distinguishes what the text says from suggested connections. No particular symbolic meaning is assigned to these branching drawings here.

Insects and wing imagery

Compare the profile insect, the Mayfly group, later winged figures, and the stippled drawing beneath the parable.

Insect imagery appears in several different forms across LP2. A profile drawing, opposed figures, a detached wing, and the stippled figure beneath the final parable offer different visual evidence. This guide brings selected examples together so they can be compared without assuming that they depict the same animal.
The profile drawing on LP2-14
Below the text at the right of LP2-14 is a sideways insect drawing. The body is segmented, a veined wing rises above it, and long curved appendages extend from its rear. The narrow branching drawing continues down the opposite margin. This combination makes the page recognizable even without reading its runes.LP2-14 — profile insect beside the branching margin. Open reader
The “Mayfly” group: LP2-23–26
The community groups LP2-23–26 under “Mayfly.” LP2-23 opens with five large dots above the text. On LP2-24–26, elongated insect-like figures flank the text on both sides. Their upper and lower parts oppose one another, which makes orientation a useful feature to record before comparing the drawings.LP2-23 — five dots above the opening text. Open readerLP2-24 — opposed figures beside the text. Open readerLP2-25 — the figures beside another text layout. Open readerLP2-26 — the final page of the community group. Open reader
The browsing name does not prove a species identification. Nor does it mean that a complete insect drawing appears on every page in the named group. The dot inventory separately records the LP2-23 arrangement.
Winged figures on later pages
LP2-53 and LP2-55 show dark winged figures beneath their text, within the surrounding curled borders. LP2-55 also has a pale tree-shaped drawing above its insect. On LP2-57, the figure is built from a dense vertical body and scattered marks extending into wing-like areas. Its rendering differs visibly from the outlined and shaded figures on pages 53 and 55.LP2-53 — winged figure beneath the red passage. Open readerLP2-55 — pale tree above a winged figure. Open readerLP2-57 — stippled figure beneath the parable. Open reader
A resemblance between two figures is a starting point for comparison. To claim that they reuse one source, compare corresponding contours, internal details, and proportions after stating any scaling or reflection. Repeated subject matter alone is insufficient.
The detached wing
LP2-27 places a long, veined wing above the red opening text. It is useful to inspect that wing separately from the whole-insect drawings. The Wing and Tree guide follows the LP2-27–32 group from this image to the tree-shaped drawing on its last page.
Connecting the images with the text
The known Welcome and final parable use the word instar. An instar is a stage between molts, not the name of a species. The parable’s language of tunneling, shedding, and emergence makes an insect comparison relevant, but it does not identify every drawing in the book as a cicada.
This distinction leaves room for close reading. Ask which visual features accompany a readable passage, then ask how the passage uses its biological analogy. On unsolved pages, there is no established reading to supply that same context.
What a defensible identification needs
	Evidence to retain	Why it matters
	The original page and an unmodified region	Shows which features are actually present, including faint lines and cropping
	A named comparison source	Lets another reader inspect the proposed illustration or anatomical reference
	Matching and nonmatching details	Prevents a general silhouette from outweighing contradictory features
	Orientation and transformations	Explains any rotation, reflection, stretching, or contrast changes used in the comparison
For an artwork-source attribution, a matching historical illustration is stronger evidence than a broad biological resemblance. For a species claim, diagnostic anatomy matters more than the puzzle’s name. Neither kind of identification automatically determines a cipher operation.
Sources and scope
Observations refer to the preserved JPEGs linked through the page records. Those records provide original files, SHA-256 hashes, and pinned public archive sources. Group names follow the Cicada Solvers LP2 index; they are community browsing labels, not decrypted chapter headings. Previews are cropped: open the reader to inspect complete pages.
This is a selected visual inventory, not an exhaustive survey of every insect depiction in Cicada 3301’s puzzles.

Wing and Tree: LP2-27–32

Follow the detached wing and tree-shaped drawing at the endpoints of the LP2-27–32 group, with all intervening pages.

“Wing & Tree” is the community name for LP2-27–32. The group begins with a detached, veined wing above the text on LP2-27 and ends with a soft-edged tree-shaped drawing below the text on LP2-32. Looking at the two endpoints makes the browsing name much easier to understand.
The illustrated endpointsLP2-27 — a detached wing above the runes. Open readerLP2-32 — a tree-shaped drawing below the runes. Open reader
The wing has a dark outer boundary and a network of internal lines. The tree-shaped drawing has a dark central trunk-like form and branching extensions, with much softer edges. These descriptions concern appearance; they do not establish a species, a source illustration, or an intended mathematical structure.
The pages between them
LP2-28–31 carry the intervening runic text. Keep these pages in view when proposing a section-wide operation: a rule that uses only the illustrated endpoints still needs to explain how it applies to the middle.LP2-28 — intervening text. Open readerLP2-29 — intervening text. Open readerLP2-30 — intervening text. Open readerLP2-31 — intervening text. Open reader
Two different kinds of branching
The wing’s internal lines form enclosed areas; the tree-shaped drawing suggests a central form with extensions. A graph can represent either tracing, but the decision about vertices and edges must be explicit. A junction, a crossing, and a closed cell are different features.
The branches and trees article defines tips, junctions, and segments as separate possible measurements. For the wing, a cell count would be another measurement: state whether the outer boundary closes a region and how faint or interrupted lines are handled. Counting a picture without those rules is difficult to reproduce.
Inspecting the soft-edged drawing
Use the original LP2-32 JPEG to inspect the tree-shaped figure. Enlarging it changes display size; it does not recover additional detail. Sharpening or thresholding can change apparent branch boundaries, so any transformed image should be shown alongside the original and identified as a derivative.
If testing a proposed source image, retain the source’s provenance and show the alignment. If measuring the manuscript alone, record the crop rectangle and test whether modest threshold changes alter the count. The image-region guide explains how to preserve those decisions.
Connecting a visual proposal to a cipher test
A test needs more than a plausible resemblance between wing veins and branches. Specify the ordered values or operation extracted from the drawing, the pages it applies to, and any reset or reading-direction rule. Record those choices before examining candidate plaintext. See documenting a reproducible attempt.
This article does not report a successful decoding or a completed geometric test. The experiment registry is the place to check documented tests once reviewed records are available.
Related images and readings
Insects and wing imagery · Branches and trees · Spiral borders · Instar and emergence in the known readings.

Circumference, identity, and emergence

Follow the term through The Loss of Divinity, the second koan, and the parable, separating textual interpretation from numerical proposals.

Circumference is one of the manuscript’s recurring terms for thinking about identity. In the contextual known readings, it appears in The Loss of Divinity, the second koan, and the final parable. The passages connect behavior, the inner voice, and the shedding of a surrounding identity, but they do not give a formal definition that settles every interpretation.

The three passages

	Section	Use of the term	Context

	The Loss of DivinityLP1-10–13	The circumference practices three behaviors	Consumption, preservation, and adherence lead to a loss of primality and divinity.

	Second koanLP1-14–15	The I is associated with its voice	A student’s thought denying an inner voice becomes the master’s example of it.

	ParableLP2-57	Circumferences are to be shed	The surrounding language concerns an instar, inward divinity, and emergence.


These are section-level references. A multi-page section is not a claim that the word appears on every listed page. The table paraphrases contextual English; use the linked complete readings and original images when checking the exact wording or rune sequence.

A pattern of dependence

The Loss of Divinity describes consumption and preservation through fears about having too little or being unable to recover what has been lost. Its criticism of adherence is more specific than a rejection of belief: both dogma and reason can be followed for the sake of belonging and being right. The passage therefore directs attention to the motive for following an idea as well as the idea itself.

The later advice about wealth complicates a simple anti-materialist reading. The text permits accumulation while rejecting attachment to possessions. Read together, these statements support an interpretation in which dependence on possessions and group approval constrains the self. That is an interpretation of the sequence, not a dictionary definition of “circumference.”

Why the second koan matters

The second koan moves from outward behavior to the voice identified as the I. The student thinks that no such voice exists; the master points to that thought as the example. The structure is self-referential: an attempted denial supplies the instance being denied.

This makes the circumference more than a literal physical perimeter in that dialogue. It is associated with a narrated or described identity. Yet the story does not establish that every person experiences thought in the same way, or that a particular psychological theory is its source. The koan guide follows both dialogues and distinguishes their literary structure from a historical attribution.

What changes in the parable

The parable uses the plural, circumferences, beside an image of emergence. Its instar comparison gives shedding a biological counterpart: moving beyond a limiting outer form. The repeated vocabulary makes it reasonable to read this alongside the earlier behavioral and identity passages.
Read the parable beside its original image. The preview is cropped; the reader shows the complete page.

The plural does not itself tell us how many layers there are, what order to remove them in, or which cipher transformation to apply. Those would be additional hypotheses. The text provides a recurring metaphor; a computational proposal still needs an explicit operation.

The geometric word and a numerical hypothesis

In geometry, circumference concerns a circle’s boundary or its length. For a circle of radius r, the length is 2πr. The manuscript’s use of the word does not supply a radius, a unit, or an instruction to calculate π. A solver proposing such a connection must identify which page data represent those quantities.

The same caution applies to “primality” in The Loss of Divinity. Its proximity to the manuscript’s prime-valued alphabet makes a numerical comparison worth stating carefully, but it does not specify whether to use rune indices, prime values, word totals, or something else. The prime-sum guide explains how to make a proposed calculation reproducible.

For an external comparison, see Blake’s outward circumference of energy. The shared term deserves attention, but the two works assign it different roles.

Find the occurrences yourself

The known-reading concordance searches contextual sections without double-counting a section for each of its pages:

python scripts/reading_concordance.py circumference
python scripts/reading_concordance.py circumference --prefix

The first command finds two exact-word occurrences. The second also finds CIRCUMFERENCES in the parable, giving three occurrences. Prefix matching is an explicit choice; the tool does not silently stem words or infer synonyms. Positions refer to contextual words, not runes.

Sources and related reading

This account uses the known-reading compilation, its recorded contextual English, and the original page records linked from the complete readings. It makes an internal textual comparison, not an attribution to a particular religion or philosophical school. Continue with philosophical themes, the koans, and instar and emergence.

Search the known readings: a concordance

Find words and phrases across nine contextual readings, with reproducible counts, surrounding text, and source hashes.

A concordance locates a word or phrase and shows its surrounding text. This tool searches the nine contextual known-reading sections in Liberpedia. It is useful for comparing terms such as circumference, divinity, self, and instar without relying on memory or repeatedly opening every section.

Run a lookup

Extract the reference-data ZIP, keep its folders together, and run these commands from the extracted directory with Python 3. No extra Python package, network connection, or AI service is needed.

python scripts/reading_concordance.py circumference
python scripts/reading_concordance.py circumference --prefix
python scripts/reading_concordance.py "voice inside your head"
python scripts/reading_concordance.py instar --context 15

Exact search matches whole words or contiguous word sequences, ignoring case and most punctuation. Prefix search accepts one word and matches words that begin with it. Thus circumference --prefix includes the plural, while an exact query does not. Internal apostrophes are retained, so DON'T stays one word; a typographic apostrophe is normalized to the same character.

Read the result

Each hit gives a section ID, its page range, a one-based contextual word position, and the matched text in brackets. The surrounding text is limited by --context, which accepts 0–50 words on each side.

loss-of-divinity (lp1-10, lp1-11, lp1-12, lp1-13), word 6
THE LOSS OF DIVINITY THE [CIRCUMFERENCE] PRACTICES THREE BEHAVIORS ...

This shortened example illustrates the output; the command prints its actual context rather than an ellipsis. A section range does not identify the exact page holding the word. Open the complete reading to compare its literal page outputs and original images.

What is being searched?

	Included	Outside this search
	One contextual English reading for each of nine sections	Unsolved ciphertext, artwork, and OutGuess messages
	Whole-word and contiguous-phrase matches	Synonyms, semantic similarity, and automatic stemming
	Contextual word positions	Rune offsets, literal prime sums, or exact image coordinates

The tool searches each section once. A four-page section is not counted four times. It also does not join the end of one section to the beginning of another when matching a phrase. A zero result means the requested token sequence was not found in this contextual compilation; it says nothing about the unsolved pages.

Contextual English expands or interprets some literal rune labels. A count in this representation is therefore not automatically a count of literal rune sequences. Use rune indices and prime values when working with the actual encoded symbols.

Save a machine-readable result

python scripts/reading_concordance.py circumference --prefix --json

The JSON output includes the query, matching mode, tokenization rule, source-file SHA-256, and every hit. To save it, redirect the output to a new filename, for example by appending > circumference-concordance.json. Shell redirection may overwrite an existing file, so choose a new name for each result you intend to preserve.

The hash identifies the exact contextual compilation searched. It is not a signature or evidence that the contextual rendering is an original manuscript file. Read the checksum guide for that distinction.

Check the implementation

python scripts/test_reading_concordance.py

The checks cover the three circumference passages, singular-versus-prefix matching, phrase boundaries between sections, apostrophes, and duplicate section rejection. The script and tests are included in the reference-data bundle.

Files and provenance

Lookup script · Checks · Contextual source compilation. The source record retains its own provenance and explains how contextual English differs from literal transliteration.

Sources, related references, and files
https://jelliottdev.github.io/downloads/reference-data.zip

Primality and divinity

Trace the words through The Loss of Divinity and the parable, then distinguish the mathematical definition from literary interpretation.

Primality and divinity meet in a specific claim in The Loss of Divinity: consumption, preservation, and adherence cause the loss of primality, and consequently divinity. The later parable describes divinity as something to find within. Reading the passages together gives the words a context; it does not turn them into a complete philosophical system or a cipher instruction.

Where the words occur

	Known-reading section	Contextual word position	What occurs there

	The Loss of DivinityLP1-10–13	4	DIVINITY in the section heading.

	The Loss of Divinity	15	The opening statement introduces behaviors that cause its loss.

	The Loss of Divinity	152 and 156	PRIMALITY followed by DIVINITY in the concluding explanation of those behaviors.

	ParableLP2-57	17	DIVINITY is described as within, between shedding circumferences and emerging.


The current compilation therefore contains one exact occurrence of PRIMALITY and four of DIVINITY, including the heading. These are positions in contextual English, counted from one at the start of each section. They are not rune positions, and a section spanning LP1-10–13 does not place each occurrence on all four pages.

What the passage actually argues

The sequence matters. Consumption is linked to perceived scarcity and fear of future inability to obtain what is needed. Preservation is linked to fear of being unable to regain what is lost. Adherence is linked to wanting to belong and be right. The text treats both dogma and reason as things that can be followed for that last motive. Its argument concerns dependence on possession and approval, rather than simply listing disfavored objects or beliefs.

	Step in the text	Connection

	Consumption · preservation · adherence	Behaviors assigned to the circumference.

	Loss of primality	The stated consequence of those behaviors.

	Loss of divinity	Presented as following from that loss of primality.


This table follows the passage’s argument, not an experimentally established causal chain. The text does not define a measurable quantity called divinity. Nor does its advice reduce to giving up possessions: the same section advises accumulating wealth while avoiding attachment to it. That distinction makes autonomy or freedom from dependence a plausible reading of what is being lost.

What primality means mathematically

An integer is prime when it is greater than one and has exactly two positive divisors: one and itself. For example, 13 has only 1 and 13; 15 also has 3 and 5, so 15 is composite. One is neither prime nor composite. “Indivisible” is a useful shorthand only if it means that there is no factorization into two integers both greater than one.

Gematria Primus assigns the first 29 primes to its 29 runes. Every individual rune value is therefore prime by construction. That does not make a word total prime: the F and U values, 2 and 3, sum to 5, while U and TH, 3 and 5, sum to 8. A property of each term need not survive addition.

There is thus a real mathematical context for the manuscript’s choice of vocabulary. But the statement about losing primality does not identify a number, a sum, or an operation. Moving from its wording to a calculation requires a further proposal. The prime-sum guide shows why the text layer, rune values, and boundaries all matter.

A mathematical metaphor, or something more?

One possible interpretation is that primality suggests an identity that cannot be factored into the possessions, affiliations, and descriptions attached to it. This can be compared with the first koan, where successive descriptions fail to answer who the student is. It is an analogy: people are not integers, and the manuscript does not explicitly equate a possession or affiliation with a factor.

A broader reading treats primality as an original or undivided condition, without requiring a literal arithmetic operation. The known passage does not settle between these interpretations. A useful comparison should explain the actual wording and its neighboring sentences, rather than relying on the word “prime” alone.

Likewise, “divinity within” permits an interpretation involving inward discovery, but does not identify a deity, religious school, or historical source. A proposed outside influence needs a specific textual or visual comparison. See outside works and attribution for the stronger and weaker kinds of connection already documented.

The Blake comparison examines a specific passage about inward deities and explains how its account differs from the manuscript’s parable.

How the parable changes the emphasis
LP2-57: the parable places inward divinity beside shedding and emergence. Open the reader for the complete image.

The earlier section describes a loss. The parable describes a movement: shed circumferences, find divinity within, and emerge. This gives the shared vocabulary a different role. Divinity is not only something the text says can be lost; it is also something its concluding parable asks the reader to discover.

The instar image supplies the biological comparison, while the circumference article follows the identity language through the second koan. Together these links let a reader examine the recurring terms without assuming that every drawing or sentence encodes the same operation.

Check the occurrences and arithmetic separately

Extract the reference-data ZIP and run these commands from its folder with Python 3. The concordance guide explains the matching and word-position rules.

python scripts/reading_concordance.py primality --context 18
python scripts/reading_concordance.py divinity --context 8
python scripts/reproduce_prime_sums.py

The first two commands locate vocabulary in the nine contextual sections. The third reproduces the separately documented sums using decoded rune sequences. A contextual word count is not an input to that sum calculation. Keeping the checks separate prevents expanded English spellings from silently changing the arithmetic.

Sources and further reading

The occurrence table and close reading use the known-reading compilation, especially The Loss of Divinity and LP2-57. The mathematical examples use the published rune values. Interpretations above are editorial comparisons, not additional decoded content. For actual numerical results, continue with prime sums, emirps, and spelling and prime sums.

Rubrication: red lettering, numbers, and boundaries

Compare different uses of red in the manuscript and record color, text, and proposed cipher boundaries separately.

Rubrication is the use of red or otherwise distinguished lettering to help organize a manuscript. In Liber Primus, red appears in headings, larger opening marks, punctuation-like clusters, and decimal numbers. Those uses need to be recorded separately: a red number in a panel is not the same kind of feature as a red heading.

What does the term mean?

The Getty’s manuscript terminology entry includes headings, initials, titles, and other distinguished text used to guide readers through a page. Its Vidal Mayor lesson shows a red heading introducing a book within a larger work. This historical terminology helps describe a visual practice; it does not date Liber Primus or identify its maker.

A heading is identified by its position and function, while red lettering describes its appearance. A decoded title may establish a heading’s meaning. Color alone does not. For an unsolved passage, report the visible color and rune sequence before assigning a title.

Three different uses of red

LP2-15: red runes above the panel; 3299 is the panel’s only red entry.
LP2-36: a red decimal 1 at the left of a text block.
LP2-57: red opening text, an enlarged angular mark, and red dot clusters.


These previews are cropped. Open the reader to inspect each complete original. They illustrate different roles for color, not an exhaustive inventory of every red mark in the book.

LP2-15 is especially useful because the rune heading and number panel occur on the same page. The panel guide records all sixteen numbers and the heading. The red 3299 is an observable distinction; interpreting it as a key, ordinal, or instruction requires an additional rule. Likewise, a transliterated red rune group is not automatically decoded English.

LP2-57 provides a known-reading comparison. Its opening is read as PARABLE in the documented direct reading. That interpretation is supported by the recorded reading, not inferred from red alone. The prime-sum guide separately distinguishes the heading from three body segments and explains how including it changes the total.

Can color mark a cipher boundary?

It can motivate a boundary hypothesis. A red heading followed by black body text gives a visible division worth checking. But several possibilities remain: the heading and body might share one transformation, use different transformations, or treat the heading as unencrypted. The image does not choose among them.

For a repeating-key proposal, even “skip the heading” is incomplete. Does the skipped heading consume key positions? Does the key restart at the next block or continue across it? The interruptions guide explains why the same visible boundary can lead to different outputs under different advancement rules.

The same issue affects measurements. The published whole-page IoC baseline includes archived rune headings. A body-only measurement would be a different input, not a corrected version of the baseline. Specify which rune positions were removed so another researcher can reproduce the comparison.

How to document a red feature


Identify the release and page, then open the original JPEG from its download record. Keep the image checksum with the observation.

Describe the feature’s location and type: heading, individual rune, number, dot cluster, or drawing. Do not merge unlike features into one “red text” stream without saying so.

Record the exact glyph sequence or decimal digits and its boundaries. If a crop is used, retain the full-image coordinates; the image-region guide explains that workflow.

Keep visible appearance separate from interpretation. “3299 is red” and “3299 selects a prime” are different claims.

For an extraction by pixel color, publish the thresholds, treatment of mixed edge pixels, and resulting mask. Check the mask against the original before treating it as a transcription.


A plain rune text file need not preserve color or layout. Do not assume that a punctuation character in an archive identifies a red mark. Compare the transcription conventions and original image, especially when proposing to extract only red material.

Sources and related subjects

Terminology: the Getty sources linked above. Examples: original page records for LP2-15, LP2-36, and LP2-57, with the LP2-15 observations and LP2-57 known reading already recorded in this wiki. Continue with dots and punctuation, the cuneiform-like page group, or the illustrated page index.

Welcome, Pilgrim: complete reading

Vigenère; LP1-03, LP1-04. Literal pages, contextual text, and exact reproduction.

This known section covers LP1-03 · LP1-04, in that order. The literal readings below preserve individual page boundaries. The contextual English at the end describes the whole section.
Method and reproduction
Vigenère: worked explanation. The recorded transformation is p = (c − key[j mod key length]) mod 29, using zero-based positions in the 29-rune alphabet.
Key indices: 23, 10, 1, 10, 9, 10, 16, 26.
Start at sequence position 0. Carry the sequence across the listed page boundaries. Non-rune characters do not consume key positions.
Copy these zero-based rune ordinals without advancing the sequence: 48, 74, 84, 132, 159, 160, 250, 421, 443, 465, 514. See interruptions and counting conventions; these recorded positions are not a universal rule for other pages.
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py welcome
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py welcome --trace

THE LOSS OF DIVINITY THE CIRCUMFERENCE PRACTICES THREE BEHAVIORS WHICH CAUSE THE LOSS OF DIVINITY CONSUMPTION WE CONSUME TOO MUCH BECAUSE WE BELIEVE THE FOLLOWING TWO ERRORS WITHIN THE DECEPTION 1 WE DO NOT HAVE ENOUGH, OR THERE IS NOT ENOUGH 2 WE HAVE WHAT WE HAVE NOW BY LUCK; AND WE WILL NOT BE STRONG ENOUGH LATER TO OBTAIN WHAT WE NEED MOST THINGS ARE NOT WORTH CONSUMING PRESERVATION WE PRESERVE THINGS BECAUSE WE BELIEVE WE ARE WEAK IF WE LOSE THEM WE WILL NOT BE STRONG ENOUGH TO GAIN THEM AGAIN THIS IS THE DECEPTION MOST THINGS ARE NOT WORTH PRESERVING ADHERENCE WE FOLLOW DOGMA SO THAT WE CAN BELONG AND BE RIGHT; OR WE FOLLOW REASON SO WE CAN BELONG AND BE RIGHT THERE IS NOTHING TO BE RIGHT ABOUT; TO BELONG IS DEATH IT IS THE BEHAVIORS OF CONSUMPTION, PRESERVATION AND ADHERENCE THAT HAVE US LOSE OUR PRIMALITY, AND THUS OUR DIVINITY SOME WISDOM AMASS GREAT WEALTH NEVER BECOME ATTACHED TO WHAT YOU OWN BE PREPARED TO DESTROY ALL THAT YOU OWN AN INSTRUCTION PROGRAM YOUR MIND PROGRAM REALITY

A Koan: second section: complete reading

Vigenère; LP1-14, LP1-15. Literal pages, contextual text, and exact reproduction.

This known section covers LP1-14 · LP1-15, in that order. The literal readings below preserve individual page boundaries. The contextual English at the end describes the whole section.
For the meaning and relationship of the dialogues, read The two koans: identity and the inner voice.
Method and reproduction
Vigenère: worked explanation. The recorded transformation is p = (c − key[j mod key length]) mod 29, using zero-based positions in the 29-rune alphabet.
Key indices: 0, 10, 4, 0, 1, 19, 0, 18, 4, 18, 9, 0, 18.
Start at sequence position 0. Carry the sequence across the listed page boundaries. Non-rune characters do not consume key positions.
Copy these zero-based rune ordinals without advancing the sequence: 49, 58. See interruptions and counting conventions; these recorded positions are not a universal rule for other pages.
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py second-koan
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py second-koan --trace
